rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane west-to-east with a 24-hour period, so it appears fixed over one point on the equator. It sits at a unique altitude of 35,800 km (r = 4.22×10⁷ m) and moves at 3.07 km/s. Geostationary orbits are vital for communications and weather satellites.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Geostationary radius: r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m
Altitude: h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km
Orbital speed: v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.07 km/s

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ 'Any 24-hour satellite is geostationary.' ✅ A geostationary satellite must ALSO be equatorial, circular, and west-to-east. A geosynchronous one just matches the 24-h period.  ·  ❌ 'Geostationary orbit can be at any height above the equator.' ✅ There is exactly ONE geostationary altitude: ≈ 35,800 km. It is set by Earth's rotation period.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The key difference from geosynchronous: geostationary also requires the equatorial plane and zero inclination.  ·  Altitude 35,800 km = about 5.6 Earth radii.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Altitude: r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m; h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km.  ·  Speed: v = 2πr/T ≈ 3.07 km/s.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'A geostationary satellite stays above one spot because it has no gravity.' ✅ It stays because its orbital period exactly equals Earth's rotation; gravity still holds it in orbit at v ≈ 3.07 km/s.  ·  ❌ 'The satellite is stationary in space.' ✅ It moves at 3.07 km/s; it is stationary only relative to the rotating Earth.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive the geostationary orbital radius from T = 24 h.  ·  Compute altitude, speed and angular speed of the orbit.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Memorise: geostationary altitude ≈ 36,000 km (35,800 km more precisely).  ·  From T to r: r = (GMT²/4π²)^(1/3) — plug 86400 s directly.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: A geostationary satellite is equatorial, west-to-east, and has T = 24 h.  ·  Its radius r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m; altitude ≈ 35,800 km.  ·  v ≈ 3.07 km/s; it appears fixed over one equator point.  ·  Geostationary orbits are unique — one height satisfies T = 24 h.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: A geostationary satellite orbits in the equatorial plane, west-to-east, with T = 24 h.  ·  Its unique altitude is ≈ 35,800 km (r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m).  ·  v ≈ 3.07 km/s — matches Earth's rotation, so it appears fixed overhead.  ·  Applications: communication, broadcasting, weather satellites.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Arthur C. Clarke proposed the geostationary orbit in 1945 (in Wireless World); it is sometimes called the Clarke orbit.  ·  The first geostationary satellite was Syncom 3 (1964), used to broadcast the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.

rows.text: Why must a geostationary satellite lie in the equatorial plane?  ·  Distinguish between geostationary and geosynchronous satellites with a diagram.  ·  Find the total energy and kinetic energy of a 2000 kg satellite in geostationary orbit.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Geosynchronous vs geostationary distinction appears in MCQs.  ·  Applications (telecom, weather, broadcasting) are direct marks.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Period: exactly 24 hours (matches Earth's rotation).  ·  Angular speed: ω = 2π/86400 ≈ 7.27×10⁻⁵ rad/s, equal to Earth's.

rows.text: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of: → B  ·  The altitude of a geostationary satellite is approximately: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Geostationary satellite:** a satellite that appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's equator. It must satisfy three conditions: (1) orbit in the plane of the equator (equatorial plane), (2) orbit in the same direction as Earth's rotation (west → east), and (3) have a period exactly equal to Earth's rotation period (T = 24 hours).  ·  **Height above Earth:** using T = 2π√(r³/GM) with T = 86400 s → r ≈ 4.22×10⁷ m from the centre → altitude h = r − R ≈ 35,800 km above the surface. This is about 5.6 Earth radii.  ·  **Orbital speed:** v₀ = 2πr/T = 2π×4.22×10⁷/86400 ≈ 3.07 km/s. It matches Earth's angular speed: the satellite and the point below rotate together, so the satellite hangs over the same longitude.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Used for communications, broadcasting and weather satellites.  ·  Angular speed: ω = 2π/T_Earth ≈ 7.27×10⁻⁵ rad/s  ·  Energy: U = −GMm/r; E_total = −GMm/2r

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Geosynchronous ≠ geostationary — geosynchronous only matches the period.  ·  ❌ 'At high latitudes people see it overhead.' ✅ A geostationary satellite is always over the equator — at high latitudes it appears low on the horizon, and near the poles it is not visible at all.  ·  ❌ 'The Moon is a geostationary satellite.' ✅ The Moon has a 27.3-day period and an inclined orbit — it is not geostationary.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: View: always over the SAME point on the equator — ideal for fixed dish antennas.  ·  At high latitudes geostationary satellites appear low on the horizon.  ·  To reach geostationary orbit rockets use a transfer ellipse + apogee burn.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB asks to compute the geostationary radius from the period or vice versa.  ·  Geostationary = equatorial + circular + west-to-east + 24-h period.  ·  Unique altitude: 35,800 km; unique radius: 4.22×10⁷ m.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The satellite appears fixed above one point on the equator.  ·  v ≈ 3.07 km/s; ω matches Earth's rotation (7.27×10⁻⁵ rad/s).  ·  Geosynchronous is a 24-h orbit but not necessarily equatorial.
